index.blurb: CNC machining, laser marking, vision inspection and robot assembly on one closed loop. The line most programs start with.

compare.processes: CNC machining, laser marking, vision inspection, robot assembly, packing

page.h1: Every flashlight starts as a bar of aluminum.
page.sub: Bar stock goes in at one end; a tested, boxed flashlight comes out at the other. CNC turning and milling, laser marking, vision inspection, robot assembly and packing on one closed loop, fed by an automated warehouse and a mobile robot.
page.description: The Flashlight production line at Phoenix Industrial Labs: an aluminum flashlight machined, marked, inspected, assembled by robot and packed by students on one closed loop, fed by an automated warehouse and a mobile robot.
page.image_alt: Flashlight production line: fenced robot cells, CNC machines, conveyors, and a control station
facts: process stations on one conveyor loop

route.p: Ten stops from a bar of aluminum to a boxed flashlight back on the shelf.
steps: An order arrives at the control and display center, which releases the job and follows it around the loop.
The automated warehouse holds bar stock, components and finished flashlights on smart pallets. The mobile robot carries a pallet to the loop.
A CNC lathe turns the body from bar stock: the outside profile, the thread and the bore.
A CNC mill cuts the grip pattern and the cap flats. A robot loads and unloads both machines.
Laser marking adds the logo and the order code, so every flashlight can be traced to the order that made it.
A vision system checks the machined faces and the marking before any component goes in.
A robot fits the LED module, the switch and the cap; a press seats the lens.
The flashlight is switched on under a light sensor. Anything dim or dark is set aside.
The flashlight is boxed at the packaging station.
An inkjet prints the order code on the box, a scanner reads it back, and the finished order rides the mobile robot to the warehouse.

items: Real machines
The lathe, the mill, the robots, the controllers and the vision system are industrial products, so the line can take on outside machining work as well as teaching.
Modular by design
Every station stands on casters with leveling feet. Run the machining cell on its own for a lesson, or join the whole loop.
A digital twin
The whole line exists in simulation. Students program and commission it virtually first, then move to the real machines.
Four zones
Storage and logistics, the machining and assembly area, a digital-twin teaching area, and the control and display center.

skills.p: Machining, robotics, controls and logistics work, grouped by what a technician actually touches.
groups: CNC
Turning and milling, tool offsets, CAD/CAM and part programs, first-article inspection.
Robots
Machine tending, assembly programming, grippers and end-of-arm tooling, robot and PLC handshakes.
Controls
PLC programming, HMI screens, fieldbus and industrial networking, sensors and detection.
Quality
Vision inspection, gauging the machined faces, light testing, and tracing a defect back to its station.
Logistics
The automated warehouse and the mobile robot: operation, communication, path planning, and RFID tracking.
Maintenance
Coolant and chip handling, spindle and axis checks, pneumatics, and keeping an automated loop running.
skills.more: This is the floor where semesters three to five happen.

compare.product: Desk pen holder, assembled and marked
compare.processes: Processing, assembly, marking, testing, packaging, storage

page.h1: An everyday object, made the industrial way.
page.sub: A desk pen holder is simple enough to understand in a morning and complete enough to need every part of a production line: processing, assembly, marking, testing, packing and storage, one module per step.
page.description: The Pen Holder production line at Phoenix Industrial Labs: a desk pen holder processed, assembled, marked, tested and packed by students on a modular line, with an automated store at the end.
page.image_alt: Pen holder production line on a factory floor
facts: process stations on one conveyor loop

route.p: Eight stops from a blank to a boxed pen holder back on the shelf.
steps: An order arrives at the control and display center, which releases the job and follows it around the loop.
The automated store holds blanks, inserts and finished pen holders on pallets. One pallet is called onto the loop per order.
A compact machining station drills the pen bores and chamfers the edges of the blank.
A pick-and-place module fits the base, the insert and the felt pad, and a press seats them.
Laser marking adds a name or a logo and the order code.
A vision check confirms the fit and the marking; a gauge checks that each bore is to size.
The pen holder is boxed at the packaging station.
An inkjet prints the order code on the box, a scanner reads it back, and the finished order returns to the store.

items: Real machines
Industrial controllers, drives, sensors and a vision system on every module, so what students learn transfers straight to a plant floor.
Modular by design
Six stations on casters. Teach one module on its own, pair two, or run the full line; every module has its own controller.
A digital twin
The line exists in simulation, so students can program a sequence and prove it virtually before loading it on the real stations.
The smallest footprint
The line that fits a classroom-sized room, which makes it the usual first floor for a program that is starting out.

skills.p: Mechanical, electrical, pneumatic and controls work, grouped by what a technician actually touches.
groups: Controls
PLC programming, HMI screens, sequencing a station, fieldbus and industrial networking.
Pneumatics
Cylinders, valves, grippers and vacuum pick-up, and the circuits behind them.
Sensors
Photoelectric, inductive and capacitive sensing, RFID on the pallets, and a first machine-vision job.
Motion
Conveyors, stepper and servo axes, and the pick-and-place module.
Quality
Vision checks, gauging, and tracing a defect back to its station.
Maintenance
Daily start-up and shutdown, fault finding, recovering a stopped line, and preventive maintenance.

compare.processes: Robot assembly, vision inspection, process control, packing, automated warehouse

page.h1: Made to order, right down to the corners.
page.sub: A frame is machined, its ornaments are printed, and robots put it together under a camera that checks every corner. Machining, 3D printing, robot assembly, vision inspection and packing on one loop, fed from an automated warehouse.
page.description: The Photo Frame production line at Phoenix Industrial Labs: a photo frame machined, printed, assembled by robot, inspected and packed by students on one conveyor loop, fed from an automated warehouse.
page.image_alt: Photo frame production line: automated warehouse, robots, CNC, 3D printing, assembly and packing
facts: process stations on one conveyor loop

route.p: Eight stops from a blank and a spool of filament to a boxed frame back on the shelf.
steps: A customer's size and design arrive at the control and display center, which releases the job and follows it around the loop.
The automated warehouse holds frame blanks, backs and finished frames on smart pallets. A pallet is picked for each order.
A CNC router cuts the frame front to size and engraves the design into it.
3D printers make the corner pieces and the stand while the front is being machined, so both arrive at assembly together.
A robot fits the glass, the back and the stand, and snaps the printed corners into place.
A vision system checks every corner, the glass and the engraving before the frame is packed.
The frame is boxed at the packaging station.
An inkjet prints the order code on the box, a scanner reads it back, and the finished order returns to the warehouse.

items: Real machines
The router, the printers, the robot, the controllers and the vision system are industrial products, so the line can make real frames for real customers.
Modular by design
Every station stands on casters with leveling feet. Run the printing cell or the robot cell on its own, or join the whole loop.
A digital twin
The whole line exists in simulation. Students program and commission it virtually first, then move to the real machines.
Two ways to make a part
Subtractive on the router and additive on the printers, side by side, so students see where each one earns its place.

PLC programming, HMI screens, fieldbus and industrial networking, sensors and detection.

CNC and printing
Router programs and tool offsets, slicing and print setup, CAD for both.
Quality
Vision inspection, limit samples, and tracing a defect back to its station.
Logistics
The automated warehouse and the pallet loop: operation, communication, and RFID tracking.
Maintenance
Printer and router upkeep, pneumatics, fault finding, and keeping an automated loop running.

index.blurb: A real bottling line: filling, capping, process control, a palletizing robot and automated storage.

compare.processes: Rinsing, filling, capping, labeling, process control, robot palletizing, automated storage

page.h1: Clean water, filled, capped and palletized.
page.sub: The one line on the floor that is a process as much as a product: water is purified, bottles are rinsed, filled, capped and labeled under continuous control, and a robot stacks the cases for the warehouse.
page.description: The Purified Water production line at Phoenix Industrial Labs: a real bottling line where students purify, rinse, fill, cap, inspect and label bottled water, palletize it by robot and store it automatically.
page.image_alt: Purified water bottling line: filling, capping, palletizing robot, and automated storage
facts: process stations on one conveyor loop

route.p: Nine stops from a tank of raw water to a pallet of cases on the rack.
steps: A batch is scheduled at the control and display center, which sets the recipe and watches every loop of the process.
The automated warehouse holds empty bottles, caps and labels, and takes the finished pallets back. The mobile robot runs between it and the line.
A small treatment skid filters the water; pressure, flow and conductivity are controlled and logged like any process plant.
Bottles are unscrambled, inverted and rinsed before anything goes in them.
A filling head doses each bottle by level; the loop is tuned by students, not set by the factory.
Caps are fed, placed and torqued, and the torque is logged against the bottle.
A vision system checks fill level, cap seating and label placement. Rejects leave the line automatically.
The label is applied and the batch code printed on it, so a bottle can be traced to its batch and its tank.
Bottles are case-packed and a robot stacks the cases on a pallet, which rides the mobile robot to the warehouse.

items: Real machines
The treatment skid, the filler, the capper, the labeler, the robot and the controls are industrial products, so the line can bottle for real.
Modular by design
Every station stands on casters with leveling feet. Run the process skid on its own for a controls lesson, or the whole line for a shift.
A digital twin
The whole line exists in simulation, process loops included, so students tune and commission it virtually first.
Food-grade handling
Stainless contact parts, sanitary fittings and a clean-in-place routine, so the habits of a food or pharma floor are taught from day one.

skills.p: Process control, controls, robotics and quality work, grouped by what a technician actually touches.
groups: Process control
Level, flow, pressure and conductivity loops, PID tuning, recipes and batch records.
Controls
PLC programming, HMI screens, fieldbus and industrial networking, sensors and detection.
Robots
Palletizing patterns, grippers, safety zoning, robot and PLC handshakes.
Quality
Vision inspection, fill-level and torque checks, batch traceability, and the paperwork behind it.
Logistics
The automated warehouse and the mobile robot: operation, communication, path planning, and RFID tracking.
Maintenance
Clean-in-place, sanitary fittings, pumps and valves, fault finding, and keeping a wet line running.

page.sub: A customer's design goes in; a finished, boxed lamp comes out. Laser cutting and engraving, assembly, inspection, packing and coding on one conveyor loop, fed by an automated warehouse and a mobile robot.
page.description: The Night Lamp production line at Phoenix Industrial Labs: a personalized night lamp made to order by students. Laser cutting and engraving, assembly, vision inspection, packing and coding on one conveyor loop, fed by an automated warehouse and a mobile robot.
page.image_alt: Night lamp production line: automated warehouse and mobile robot at the left, laser, assembly and inspection stations along a conveyor loop, packing and coding at the right
page.image2_alt: The night lamp line seen from the other side: fenced robot cells, enclosed laser stations, the control cabinet and the conveyor loop
facts: process stations on one conveyor loop

route.p: Nine stops from a customer's design to a boxed lamp back on the shelf.
steps: A customer's design and text arrive at the control and display center, which schedules the job and follows it around the loop.
The automated warehouse holds blanks and finished lamps on smart pallets. It picks a blank, and the mobile robot carries the pallet to the conveyor loop.
A laser cuts the lamp panel to shape and engraves the customer's design into it.
Laser marking adds the order code, so every lamp can be traced back to the order that made it.
At the assembly station the engraved panel meets its holder and becomes a lamp.
An in-line vision system checks the engraving and the assembly before anything is packed.
The lamp is boxed at the packaging station.
An inkjet prints the order code on the box, and a scanner reads it back to close the loop on traceability.
The finished order rides the mobile robot back to the warehouse, ready for pickup, and the job closes on the display center.

A digital twin

Four zones
Storage and logistics, the production area, a digital-twin teaching area, and the control and display center.
